subject: Action required: your password expires in 24 hours
top_finding: A link points at a lookalike domain

message.subject: Action required: your password expires in 24 hours
message.excerpt:
Dear user,
Your 
Microsoft 365
 password expires 
today
. Sign in to keep the same password.
https://login.microsoftonline.com/keep-password
If you do not act within 24 hours your account will be suspended.

findings.title: A link points at a lookalike domain
evidence: Link to login[.]microsoftonline[.]com[.]session-verify[.]example has microsoftonline[.]com at the front, but the real domain is session-verify[.]example (imitating Microsoft)
findings.lesson: Hover before you click. The link's domain, not its text, tells you where you'll land.

findings.title: Sender domain imitates a known domain
evidence: Sender domain micr0soft-support[.]example reads like microsoft[.]com once lookalike characters are folded (imitating Microsoft)
findings.lesson: Read the domain letter by letter. Attackers register names that look right at a glance.

findings.title: Link text shows one site, link goes to another
findings.lesson: What a link says and where it goes can differ. Hover to see the real destination before clicking.

findings.title: Display name poses as a brand
evidence: Display name "Microsoft 365 Support" claims Microsoft, sent from micr0soft-support[.]example
findings.lesson: The name on a message is free text. Check the address, not just who it says it is.

findings.title: Asks you to sign in, and fast
evidence: Wording asks for credentials under pressure: "sign in"; "login"; "within 24 hours"; "account will be suspended"
findings.lesson: Pressure plus a login request is the classic pairing. Pause, then go to the site on your own.

findings.title: Generic greeting on an account message
evidence: Greets a 'valued customer/user' while asking about account access
findings.lesson: Messages from a service you use usually know your name. 'Dear customer' is a tell.
